e-632.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
e-632.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = \cos(3\theta)$ and the lines $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/350a721c254dab3a8acb2ae54ca5be0bcde6ab036e6936939194c57ae55fe4ff.png)
e-632.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-633.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
e-633.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 1+2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/6bfa0990b560bcb09f2a9eb0b9542296f2a8f1c196b6740702e81c59941d66c5.png)
e-633.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-6822.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
e-6822.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/d7b39805131dc562e233d49a84f69d30e80ca29cb9443012032d18fdb4512054.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ as shown above.
e-6822.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4+8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}) \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-1 \\  & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(3θ) for 2π3≤θ≤π?

a
 92∫2π/3πsin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
 12∫π/22π/3sin⁡(3θ)dθ
c
 23∫2π/3πsin2⁡(9θ)dθ
d
 32∫π/3πsin2⁡(θ)dθ
e
 92∫π/3πsin2⁡(θ+3)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The polar area formula is A = (1/2)∫r² dθ. Substituting r = 3sin(3θ) and the bounds 2π/3 to π gives A = (9/2)∫ sin²(3θ) dθ, exactly option a.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{2\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(3θ) for 2π3≤θ≤π?

a
 92∫2π/3πsin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
 12∫π/22π/3sin⁡(3θ)dθ
c
 23∫2π/3πsin2⁡(9θ)dθ
d
 32∫π/3πsin2⁡(θ)dθ
e
 92∫π/3πsin2⁡(θ+3)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3sin⁡(3θ), θ1=2π3 and θ2=π, this gives A=12∫2π/3π(3sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=12⋅9∫2π/3πsin2⁡(3θ)dθ=92∫2π/3πsin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
content.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{2\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the area bounded by the graph of the polar curve r=3cos⁡(2θ) for π4≤θ≤3π4?

a
23∫−π/43π/4cos⁡(2θ)dθ
b
29∫π/43π/2cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
34∫π/43π/4cos2⁡(2+θ)dθ
d
 92∫π/43π/4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
12∫π/23π/4cos2⁡(θ)dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Using the polar area formula A = (1/2)∫r² dθ with r = 3cos(2θ) gives A = (9/2)∫ from π/4 to 3π/4 of cos²(2θ) dθ. This is option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by the graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}?$
after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
content.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by the graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}?$
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\pi $ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{4}(\theta {|}_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ){|}_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}((\frac{5\pi }{4}-(\pi ))+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}(\frac{\pi }{4}+0) \\  & =\frac{25\pi }{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\pi -0)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}+2(-2)-\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi -16}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=2−sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π, as shown above.

a
9π−82
b
9π+164
c
9π4
d
9π−164
e
9π−64
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=2−sin⁡θ, θ1=0 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫0π(2−sin⁡θ)2dθ=12∫0π(4−4sin⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)dθ=12(4θ|0π+4cos⁡θ|0π+12∫0π(1−cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=12(4θ|0π+4cos⁡θ|0π+12(θ|0π−sin⁡(2θ)2|0π))=12(4θ|0π+4cos⁡θ|0π+12θ|0π−sin⁡(2θ)4|0π)=94θ|0π+2cos⁡θ|0π−sin⁡(2θ)8|0π=94(π−0)+2(cos⁡(π)−cos⁡(0))−18(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(0))=9π4+2(−2)−18(0)=9π−164.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/f57ddfb02991296cbc0280272aa1a28e36cfed926dfedcd7b1955868cf83fff5.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\pi -0)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}+2(-2)-\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi -16}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=1+cos⁡(θ)4 for 0≤θ≤2π?

a
∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
b
12∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)dθ
c
12∫0π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
d
∫0π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)dθ
e
12∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The total polar area is A = (1/2)∫₀^(2π)r² dθ. Since r = 1 + cos(θ)/4 is positive throughout and traces the curve once, substituting it gives exactly option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve $r=1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4}$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ?$
after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4}$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4})}^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

after.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=1+cos⁡(θ)4 for 0≤θ≤2π?

a
∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
b
12∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)dθ
c
12∫0π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
d
∫0π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)dθ
e
12∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=1+cos⁡(θ)4, θ1=0 and θ2=2π, this gives

A=12∫02π(1+cos⁡(θ)4)2dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
content.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve $r=1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4}$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ?$
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4}$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}{4})}^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

Question 11
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=3e2θ for 0≤θ≤π.

a
98(e2π−1)
b
98(e4π−1)
c
34(eπ−1)
d
34(e2π−1)
e
34(e4π−1)
Submit

decision.explanation: Using A = (1/2)∫₀^π r² dθ gives A = (9/2)∫₀^π e^(4θ) dθ = (9/8)(e^(4π) − 1), which is option b.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3{e}^{2\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3{e}^{2\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4\theta }\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=3e2θ for 0≤θ≤π.

a
98(e2π−1)
b
98(e4π−1)
c
34(eπ−1)
d
34(e2π−1)
e
34(e4π−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3e2θ, θ1=0 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫0π(3e2θ)2dθ=92∫0πe4θdθ=92⋅14e4θ|0π=98(e4π−e0)=98(e4π−1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
content.problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3{e}^{2\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3{e}^{2\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4\theta }\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2{e}^{1-\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}(2{e}^{1-\theta })^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}4{e}^{2-2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{e}^{-2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-2\theta }}{2}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)} \\  & =-{e}^{2}({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-{e}^{2}(\frac{1}{9}-1) \\  & =\frac{8{e}^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 13
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve r=2θ+cos⁡(θ) for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫02π(θ+cos⁡(θ))2dθ
b
12∫0π(2θ+cos⁡(θ))2dθ
c
12∫0π/2(θ+cos⁡(θ))2dθ
d
12∫02π(θ+cos⁡(θ))2dθ
e
2∫0π(θ+cos⁡(θ))2dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The polar area formula is A = (1/2)∫r² dθ. Substituting r = 2θ + cos(θ) with bounds 0 to π gives exactly option b.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve $r=2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
content.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve $r=2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
content.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )={e}^{\theta +1}$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{({e}^{\theta +1})}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{2\theta +2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}(\frac{{e}^{2\theta }}{2}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{4}({e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{4}(4-1) \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
